text: The first worldview you ever learned divided people into two kinds: family inside the faith, and outsiders headed for hell.
Birthdays, the Spring Festival, the Mid-Autumn Festival—all 'heathen filth.' While other kids unwrap gifts, you kneel in prayer.
Your parents 'consecrated' your tuition money to the church, and the whole family began fasting in prayer two days a week. Hunger proved more real than any miracle.
The 'school' you attended was the basement of the cult compound, and the textbooks were photocopied transcripts of the master's sayings.
At eight years old you stood before the mass confession meeting and publicly admitted to 'harboring irreverence.' Two hundred people below the stage lamented your soul in unison.
Your parents reported your unbelieving uncle to the church. His name was never spoken at home again—nor was it ever mentioned that he taught you to ride a bike.
Running a forty-degree fever, you lay there while your parents sang hymns over you all night. Medicine is the devil's snare. You survived—but your ears never fully recovered.
For your birthday you received a betrothal contract: the elder's son, 'arranged by the Lord.'
You secretly finished a 'book of sorcery'—actually a middle-school physics textbook. So clouds are not the breath of God. A crack opened in the world.
Dragged back after skipping school, you were called out by name before the entire assembly. Three hundred pairs of eyes, three hundred needles.
The leader's portrait hung above your bed, and the last line of your bedtime prayer was always his name. Only years later did you learn this is called a cult of personality.
Your older sister was expelled from the church for 'abandoning the true way.' The whole family walked out of her life together—including you, eight years old.
The night police lights flooded the compound, you tasted chocolate for the first time at the shelter. A worker knelt down and asked your name—no one had ever asked you that before.
After the rescue you were placed mid-year into a public school. Seated in a classroom of younger kids, you stared at a math exam covered in symbols you couldn't read.
Anti-cult volunteers spent two years walking you through deprogramming. The first time you said the leader's name aloud, you waited a long while—and no lightning fell.
Your deskmate shared one earbud with you. The pop song's lyrics meant nothing—but it was the freest three minutes you had ever heard.
At eighteen, friends threw you the first birthday cake of your life. When the candles were lit, you cried without knowing why.
Applying for your ID card, you discovered that the 'home address' on your birth certificate was a room number in the compound.
Even as an adult, your heart still skips whenever people speak in unison. The counselor says it's a conditioned fear response, not weakness.
You found your exiled sister. The first thing she said when she opened the door was: 'They let you go?' You held each other and cried until dawn.
